text_fidelity_a:
Garmin nüvi 1390/1390T 4.3-Inch Bluetooth Portable GPS Navigator (Discontinued by Manufacturer) I first became enamored of the garmin company after using the one with a rental car. The ease of use and accuracy was impressive. Unfortunately, that model is no longer in production so I opted for this unit.

In general I am pleased. Easy to set up, the unit features a bright, clear screen. It is a snap to use and the directions have been unfailing accurate. I drive alot and so far have used this unit throughout New York, New Jersey, Pennsylvania, Maryland, DC and Virginia. I have had no problem with reception even while traversing mountainous regions. I appreciate the advance notice for turns and the voice command system is a convenience.

However, this unit is not flawless. The robotic voice often mispronounces street names and the voice command system seems a bit hard of hearing when it comes to addresses. I have had to pull over and type in the address. The unit does not like to deviate from its chosen route. For instance, one location I frequent in New York is accessible both by the thruway (toll road) and other non-toll main arteries. Both are about the same distance. When I want to avoid the toll route, the unit will recalculate directing that I turn around and follow the initial route multiple times before adjusting to the alternate route. A big deal, no,but annoying nonetheless. While I have not been terribly plagued by the pop ups, they are annoying and potentially unsafe. While the start up guide and manual are adequate, they are barely so. Whatever happened to detailed instructions? But my biggest gripe is the customer service. I called twice with questions and had ridicualously long waits of fifteen minutes and twenty-five minutes respectively. There is no round the clock service. The last time I called it wasnt even available all week, totally unacceptable.

So while I like this system,there is room for improvement.
text_fidelity_b: Garmin nüvi 1390/1390T 4.3-Inch Bluetooth Portable GPS Navigator (Discontinued by Manufacturer)

text_fidelity_a:
Fitbit One Wireless Activity Plus Sleep Tracker, Black I bought my Fitbit One after a considerable amount of research among the various "life activity trackers" on the market. As I read, my focus shifted from the features of the products themselves to the personal goals I intended to accomplish once I started moving around. Ultimately, this helped me make my final purchase.

As you may have found, I discovered that despite the choices available to the consumer, I did not find a particular fitness tracker that measured all daily activities equally well. Design philosophies and marketing strategies seem to conspire to confuse the subject further and make it difficult to match a particular product to your needs. However, many excellent reviews have been published by Amazon-reviewers as well as by online product-review writers which were very helpful.

In any event, I was looking for a decent pedometer and sleep monitor. I can't run anymore due to arthritis, but I do enjoy walking and was pretty sure that I am not moving around enough. I also suspected that sleep apnea was starting creep up on me and hoped that the sleep tracking function could share some insight into my sleep patterns. I do some biking and other exercises, but I wasn't all that concerned about accurately tracking those activities through the Fitbit. Other electronic gizmos cover those areas.

The Fitbit appealed to me because it is tiny and can be carried discretely. Pedometers tend to work fine, but can be bulky and clunky-looking. The Bluetooth syncing was also a big selling point allowing data entry to be very simple, although for some the data analysis may be too simple. As of this writing, the Moto Droid just became Bluetooth 4.0 compatible with Fitbit products. According to the website more smartphones and tablets are being added on the Android platform. The package came with a small pocket clip, an armband for sleep tracking, and a charger.

Since I picked this product up, from RadioShack incidentally, I have been very happy with it. The pedometer function is very accurate and works equally well at measuring flights of stairs, which is a very nice feature. The small size is great for pocket carry, particularly in the change pocket of a pair of jeans, and can be clipped to pants or shirts depending on your preference. I compared the Fitbit's ability to monitor sleep patterns with a sleep monitoring app on my Droid. Gross measures of restlessness were comparable for each and it seems that I sleep better than I thought.

I've worn this unit during other activities, but the accuracy of movement that it measures is questionable. The Fitbit One, at least, is probably best suited for walking. Nonetheless, with consistent wearing, overall activity can probably be deduced, but will have to be inferred from data recorded as "steps".

In sum, the Fitbit One seems to be the closest match to an activity-meter that meets my personal needs. That means measuring natural everyday movement, such as steps, stairs, and sleep, in a tiny sleek wireless package. It helps raise my awareness of non-structured daily activity and is an important tool for overall health.
text_fidelity_b: Fitbit One Wireless Activity Plus Sleep Tracker, Black

text_fidelity_a:
Mokata Headphone Bluetooth Wireless Over Ear On Foldable Hi-fi Stereo Headset with AUX 3.5mm Jack Cord SD Card Slot Microphone for Young Adults Cellphone TV Rechargeable Equipment B02 Red I got this set of headphones to go with our panasonic phone system in your house for our landline. Many times we get power failures so we still keep a landline. But when the power is not out, I like to use our landline for calls. Our system uses bluetooth for headsets so this is where these came in handy.

HOW ARE THESE?
These headphones are red. I love the color. they seem sturdier than expected, There is a slot in the headphones which you can insert a MicroSD card so you don't HAVE to use a player with the headphones (like phone or MP3, etc). These are bluetooth as well and have a volume button.

HOW DO THESE PERFORM?
My family is a bunch of ear phone addicted fanatics. We have some of the best and some of the worst and everything in between. When I started to try these out, I really liked them and was surprised at how loud they were. One of our kids, a daughter, grabbed the headphones to try them and loved them so much, she is getting a pair for her pottery studio to listen to her own music.

ARE THEY TOO LOUD?
I did not think these were too loud. They were controlled easily through the volume control on the headphones.

ARE THEY COMFORTABLE?
I use these mainly to talk on the phone so I don't have to cradle the phone to my head when working while talking. These are comfortable and as long as I am not SUPER active with these on, they seem to stay on fairly well. They are comfortable and my ears last about a half hour before I want to remove them. Sometimes longer.

CHARGING
These do not take long at all to charge. Within a few hours they were ready to go.

ADJUSTABLE?
These are not hard to adjust and they seem to adapt well to all of our heads.

SOUND QUALITY
The sound quality is surprisingly good with these. There is good definition and it is not muffled or out of proportion to the point that you prefer them not to be on. Let me just say that the daughter that is going to buy these is so impressed she is very excited for this price to get her own pair. She is very picky about her ear buds or headphones.

DO THEY BLOCK NOISE?
These do block outside noise well which is another great feature of these.

VOICE?
So far the voice works well with these when I use them on the phone.

THE BOTTOM LINE
For a decent set of headphones that are comfortable, block outside noise well, and do well on the phone for both listening and voice as well as music, these are a great choice. I love the red color too.

MY RATING
FIVE STARS. These are great, affordable and work well so far. I will update if anything changes.

I expected a much more light gold/pearl color earbud, and instead received an ugly flat ivory/gold pair and also look much larger in my ear than I had anticipated. As soon as I put them in, I thought to myself that they look like hearing aids, and when I saw the other person's Amazon review indicating the same, knew I wasn't crazy.

I tested them out for a bit and they were super easy to pair, sound quality seemed very good (compared to much less expensive wireless earbuds I have purchased on Amazon), and the button press controls seemed intuitive. However, I could tell they would become quite uncomfortable after extended periods of time. Not only are they large, but you have to press the buttons (especially on the left bud which controls volume and song skipping) pretty hard to get them to work, which presses them in to your ear even more, and that ends up hurting after a while. However, I will say that when I first put them in, they fit very snugly and I would not hesitate to use them for working out.

I am going to go with my first pick and try out the Samsung Galaxy Buds instead as they are supposed to have a sleeker profile than these. If I didn't already have the Galaxy Buds in mind, I would stick with the Jabras but go for the black color.

**EDIT 7/21/19**: I ended up buying the Samsung Galaxy Bud and enjoy them significantly more. Rather than buttons, they function by gestures (ie, tap once for play/pause, tap twice for next song/answer call, etc.), and you can customize what you want a long hold to do in the app that connects to the buds. In addition, they are smaller and have a much sleeker profile as I had expected!

text_fidelity_a:
PIONEER Truly Wireless in-Ear Headphones, Black, SE-C8TW(B) If you're an iphone user, you're probably wondering whether to buy these Pioneer wireless headphones or the Apple version. The Pioneer price is about 1/3 cheaper than Apple. The Pioneer earbuds fit in your ear, so you get much better sound and much better sound isolation. These are nowhere near as detailed or loud as similarly priced wired headphones, but that's true of all wireless Bluetooth earbuds. I will say the connection is stable and not noisy, so these are better than most cheap Bluetooth earbuds. There is some bass, but don't work well for bass-heavy music. Maximum volume is just OK. Battery life is only about 3 hours per charge (compared to 5 hours for Apple), then you have to put the earbuds back in the case for a 1 hour charge. 3 hours may be enough for you; you have to decide, but 5 hours is certainly going to be more interesting to most people. The charging case is much larger than the Apple charging case. The case is 3.3 inches long and 2.2 inches wide. These case is to big to fit comfortably in my pants pocket, so I would only carry it with me in a backpack or purse.

Usage is pretty simple. They paired easily with my phone as a normal Bluetooth device. The buttons on the headphones are easy to use. They are comfortable in my ears. They are secure enough so far, never feeling like they are going to fall out. They are not noticeably heavy like some earbuds can be. When in my ears, they are much less ugly than the Apple earbuds.

I would give these 5 stars for the price and performance if the sound and battery life were better. Frankly, I've tried a few different totally wireless earbuds and been less than impressed by all of them. Bluetooth headphones that have a wire connecting the two pieces can be had for much lower prices and have much better sound quality and much better battery life. Removing the wire just doesn't seem worth the downsides to me.
text_fidelity_b: PIONEER Truly Wireless in-Ear Headphones, Black, SE-C8TW(B)

text_fidelity_a:
Belkin Secure and Charge - AC Lockable Classroom Charging Station for Laptops & Tablets - Classroom Organization & iPad Charging Station - Up To 10 Devices Including iPads, Samsung Tablets & More My desk is cluttered with cords and cables for various pieces of equipment, including my laptop and my tablet. And I am constantly trying to figure out where to find an available power outlet. I was hopeful that the Belkin Store and Charge Station would be a good solution to these problems. Though it is a good idea and it does accomplish its stated purpose it has a couple of shortcomings, the largest of which is the price.

The idea of this device is very simple - it has dividers where one can put a set of tablets, laptops, even cell phones, plug them all in and keep everything neat and tidy all while using a single wall outlet. The trade-off is the size of this unit, which takes up a fair amount of desk space. It takes up about as much space as a desktop computer.

The whole unit comes with 10 outlets on a heavy-duty power strip which slide-mounts on the back. The cables then run through the unit and under a plastic baffle and out the front where they can plug into the devices to which they correspond. The concept is fairly simple and straightforward, and the implementation works - you will have less desk clutter and the cords will be a lot less likely to get tangled and knotted. However, it does mean taking the unit apart to remove a cable should the need arise, though that’s simple enough.

The power cord is nice and long which is a good thing. This addresses and issue I have had in my specific configuration where the closest available outlet is across the room, out of each from most devices. Of course, with 10 outlets available on this unit that frees up a couple of the closer outlets.

The tray and base are made of heavy-grade plastic and should hold up to years of use. I have no issues with the construction or design of this thing.

This is an expensive piece of equipment - $200 retail as I write this. I’m sorry, but that is far higher than what is reasonable. I could see an asking price of maybe $65-$75 but beyond that is simply too much. Even the sale price here on Amazon is still too high. For the same price, a power strip with a large, heavy cardboard box would serve the same purpose. The price is the single biggest problem with this unit.

I have a very difficult time recommending this unit mainly because of the price. Cutting the price in half would still make it expensive but it would be close to reasonable. If decluttering your desk is the goal and you don’t mind spending a good bit of money on an organizational system this is not a bad choice.
text_fidelity_b: Belkin Secure and Charge - AC Lockable Classroom Charging Station for Laptops & Tablets - Classroom Organization & iPad Charging Station - Up To 10 Devices Including iPads, Samsung Tablets & More

Since my monitor was so light to begin with I used the thumb bolts, which hold the viewing angle in the narrow range of movement the VESA mount allows. Had my monitor been heavier I would have probably used the hex bolts, which are a lot beefier.

Bottom line: read some of the other reviews that discuss challenges that this mount has for heavier and larger monitors. However, if you have a 24" that is in the 10-12 pound range (or less) this is all the mount that you need. text_fidelity_a:
VIZIO SB3820-C6 38-Inch 2.0 Channel Sound Bar The sound from this bar is clean, clear, crisp and LOUD! A very decent amount of BASS, with a sub woofer output should you want to connect one. I found out I ordered a longer bar than is recommended. How did I find out? The packaging for this bar states that it is for a 42" or larger TV. I purchased it for a 32" TV. The concern, I believe, is that if the speakers are too far from the TV's center it will not seem as though the audio is coming from the actors. My brain is making the leap and tricking me so all is well. I use my TV for music for the most part anyway (Comcast Music Choice and Fire TV Music).
It is disappointing that Fire TV Music has such poor audio quality since it is there that I can make personal music choices unlike Comcast. Fire TV just sounds plain bad. It did on the TV speakers and now on the bar; it is just un-listenable. Safe to call it "LOW FIDELITY"
As far as connecting an input to this bar from your TV you have many options and most all the cables you may need are included. I really liked that they included the cord to to connect the bar to a sub. This cord is over and above what is required to connect the bar to the TV...very nice touch VIZIO. Now I need to go to my storage and try to find my sub :-)
My TV only offers 2 audio outputs, head phone and optical. Included with the bar were a headphone-to-2 RCA connector cord, and a fiber optic patch cord, among others. That allowed me what would be considered the worst quality connection and the best quality connection possibilities. If you don't have OPTICAL OUT on your TV do not despair...the worst possible option (headphone-to-RCA patch cord) sounds FANTASTIC! I can detect no loss of fidelity between the two. You will not be missing out.
Now to the reason I gave it 3 stars rather than 5. The back of the remote just keeps sliding off. It is not broken in any way. Just poorly designed. I often use the sound bar in dark or nearly dark conditions. It is taking time to train myself to not go where I normally would to use the any of the buttons. So how about the POWER button? It is not the top left button on the remote as you will see and are used to on any other remote in your home. For some strange reason instead of the power button being in the far upper left of the remote they felt this was a good place to position the INPUT button. Power is upper right. Volume UP/DOWN is traditionally placed on the left side of the remote with a paddle switch or separate buttons. Located in the standard volume UP/DOWN positions are the TruVolume and the TruSurround HD. The volume UP/DOWN are located on a FLAT 1-3/8" (34.9mm) x 1-3/8" (34.9mm) multi-function EVER SO SLIGHTLY RAISED square. To be honest I can't even tell that it IS raised at all most of the time. If you go for the volume in low light you may operate any of 3 other function controls. Lastly, if you were hoping the VOLUME controls are the 2 well raised buttons on the right (traditional location) you would be wrong. Those are your BASS/TREBLE controls.
I am not sure I would buy this bar again knowing what I do now about the remote. As I said I often use the remote in low or no light. The problems I mention here may just be my own...but I doubt it. All of these tiny buttons and controls are all scrunched into a small 2-3/8" (60.3mm) x 1-3/8" (34.9mm) upper 40% of this little remote and they are not raised enough and not far apart enough to be used just by touch. I well believe that just 3 functions on the remote will account for 90% of it's use. POWER (that CAN be felt but it is in the wrong place...you'll get used to that) and the VOLUME UP/DOWN that exist on a square, fully smooth (NO tactile feedback...I'd hate to see a blind person trying to operate), 4-function piece of plastic that is raised about 1/32" (0.8mm). On the bright side for me, I found out fairly quickly that my cable box remote controls the basic functions of the sound bar. I hope you get so lucky.
Knowing what I know now I should have purchased a bar in the 28"-32" (71mm-81mm) class looking for features such as the control panel on the bar being mildly illuminated and a proper remote perhaps with illumination itself. My roommate may buy mine from me for a location that is always well lit and has a 42" TV. I'll lose $20 on the deal but I can get the absolute right bar for me.. I don't return items that are not what I would like due to my own failure in researching. So, for better or worse, the bar is mine. There is one thing you cannot fault; THIS THING SOUNDS AMAZING!
- Good Shopping!!!
text_fidelity_b: VIZIO SB3820-C6 38-Inch 2.0 Channel Sound Bar

Nomodo U Wireless Wearable Bluetooth Speaker, Rechargeable and Portable I ordered the 'Nomodo U Wireless Wearable Bluetooth Speaker, Rechargeable and Portable' for review and would like to share some of my thoughts and experiences.
First off, out of the box this Bluetooth Wireless Speaker not only looks interesting but it is beautiful. I say interesting because I have never had a Wireless Speaker like this, and I wonder where would I use it and would it be practical. Well after some time with this device I must first report that it really does sound amazing. The sound is clean and immersive. It is hard to describe the incredible sound sensation while wearing it. It is almost as if you have speakers floating on either side of your head (pointing directly to your ears) and it is nothing like I have experienced before but it is pretty cool. I have been trying to think of how this Speaker would actually fit into my life. It's not like you are wearing headphones that only you can hear. While wearing this speaker, everyone else around you can hear it too but it's just not as immersive as it is to you. It's hard to describe, but what I will say is that it really is an incredible experience. If the volume is down low you can still hear your surroundings yet when you crank it up, surprisingly your surrounding sounds seem to disappear. Personally I have decided that this would be best worn while alone in your home while doing simple household chores. Like doing dishes or folding laundry. The Nomodo U speaker stays put pretty well for the most part due to the rubber neck pad, yet if you are constantly bending over or doing anything where you are moving around a lot and twisting your head and body, it tends to need re adjusted. Sitting in bed listening to Music or listening to an audio book works really well with this device as long as you wont be disturbing your partner. As for watching movies, for me this really doesn't work. I can't find anywhere where it says what version of Bluetooth this is using but I don't think it is Bluetooth 5.0 unfortunately. There are noticeable sync issues and this just gets annoying. Speaking of the Bluetooth, it connects/pairs effortlessly to all of my devices and that is a bonus. I am disappointed however that it uses Micro USB (the cable is included btw) for charging. With this being a new device it should have USB Type C. I always have to mention this with any new devices. Call quality is acceptable. Those on the other end can hear you just fine, as long as you are not in a loud environment. This is pretty typical with most wireless headphones. Overall I do love this device and think it is a great value for what it is.
text_fidelity_b: Nomodo U Wireless Wearable Bluetooth Speaker, Rechargeable and Portable

Steiner Marine Binoculars for Adults and Kids, 7x50 Binoculars for Bird Watching, Hunting, Outdoor Sports, Wildlife Sightseeing and Concerts - Quality Performance Water-Going Optics , Black I bought these at the same time as a Steiner 7x50 Commander XP model. The Commander XP's use the same case but for triple the price have better eyepieces, coatings and optical specifications and a few additional or better accessories than the Marine model.

I compared them in terrestrial and celestial viewing but the easiest comparison is done with astronomical subjects since they really define performance clearly. The images in the Marine model merged effortless. In the Commander XP, I have difficulty merging the images. The XP's are obviously badly out of collimation. I don't care to fix this myself on binos in this price range but I was pleased that the much less costly Marine's appear to be flawless in this respect.

I evaluated the real and apparent fields of view as well as the sharpness near the edge of the field.

In the Marine model, the real field of view is reasonably wide but apparent field is quite narrow. It's not bad but it's not a spectacular vista either. In the Commander XP, the real FOV is only barely perceptibly wider. Steiner's website lists the specifications. The apparent field, which is not specified is about the same for both. The almost indiscernable extra width of real FOV does not contribute much to the value of the XP's for triple the price.

On the Marine model, I put Sirius and Jupiter in the center of the field. They each looked nice. Moving the binoculars so that the objects were farther from the center of the field I could see the image degraded about half-way to the edge of the field of view. Near the very edge, the image was appalling. Much more than half-way out of the center of the field of view, the star or planet turns from a bright point to just a smear. Near the very edge it's a dim smudge. I tried the same with the Commander XP. It was every bit as bad. I could have probably improved things a little by refocusing but that only means that the field isn't flat either.

Are the XP's better on dim objects? The optics are supposed to transmit 96% light compared to the Commander V's 95% and the Marine's 90%. I saw very little difference on dim objects like the Orion nebula or the background of the Pleides or Jupiter's moons. Again, I can't see the justification for triple the price, so I commend these Marine models over their far more costly cousins.

Both have generious eye-relief, 20mm for the Marine and 22mm for these XP's. They also have the same weight and dimensions. They're heavy but still reasonable if you're wearing a thick coat to pad your chest and a harness to keep them from swinging all over if you're moving. Also, at 7x they're reasonable for handholding. For me, 7x50 is about the limit for handholding. Heavier or higher power would be too shakey. 6x56 might be nicer if they were more common.

Where the XP is clearly better is with small details like the click-loc strap attachments (for use with Steiner straps and harnesses only), the better eyepiece covers, lens covers, focuser grips, shading eye-cups, and various doo-dads that come in the case. It comes with a flotation strap which the Marine doesn't, but I would still rather prefer a harness which neither comes with.

I bought these Porro prism binos because I thought for the high price, particularly the XP's, they should be outstanding. While roof prism binos might require fifteen hundred dollars or more to achieve optical exellence (or so I've heard), it should be easier with porros. With these, the optical quality is lacking nontheless. To be honest, I have nothing to compare them to. I've never seen better, but I was still totally underwhelmed by the performance which was only slightly better than I would expect from binoculars in the hundred dollar range. In the case of the XP's, it's a rip-off, no question. In the case of the Marine model, the value is closer to reasonable because of the far lower price. I didn't compare them to other binos in their price range. The Fujinon line would be the most similar but it would also be worthwhile to compare Nikons, even the well-regarded Monarch roof prism models which are in this price category but are totally different.
text_fidelity_b: Steiner Marine Binoculars for Adults and Kids, 7x50 Binoculars for Bird Watching, Hunting, Outdoor Sports, Wildlife Sightseeing and Concerts - Quality Performance Water-Going Optics , Black

Blink XT Home Security Camera System - 5 Camera Kit - 1st Gen I had an Arlo set-up, and while I really liked it, I was constantly changing batteries. (Busy street).
I saw these read some good reviews and liked the battery life.
Plus they take regular AA batteries. Easy to install. But the hangers are not very flexible, you are limited in how you are able to position the camera. For example, I have one camera up on the side of my carport, and I need for it to tilt down and to the left. With the provided hanger, that is not possible. I will make an adapter for this, but after th ease of positioning of the Arlos, I am disappointed.
Set-up was a breeze, after hanging them where I wanted them, I opened the mobile app, connected them to the supplied Bridge, and Wifi. Made adjustments to various app settings and done, reading instructions, hanging and set-up in under an hour. One of the nice aspects is the zones, (you can "block" areas from motion detection on individual cameras. so Doorways or street, sidewalks, etc to fit high traffic and pedestrian areas.
The presets are nice, but for some like me who have unusual areas to cover, some time and subtle adjustments will be needed.
The storage provided for free is adequate for me.
What I am not a fan of is the delay in recording, a couple seconds, but enough time for things/people to move out of camera view.

text_fidelity_a:
Sony HT-A5000 5.1.2ch Dolby Atmos Sound Bar Surround Sound Home Theater with DTS:X and 360 Spatial Sound Mapping, works with Alexa and Google Assistant,Black This arrived well packaged and without issues. I've tried out several major brand soundbars in recent years, and I've yet to find any that are as good as the Sonys, at least as a television speaker. I've already got an A7000 that I'm familiar with to compare this A5000 with. It's a step down in price and feature set, but there's more to the differences than that.

The A7000 has cloth speaker covers on top, while this A5000 has plastic. It's my impression that the sound is a bit better out of the cloth, since it provides less of a reflective barrier, but it's also hard to keep clean and safe. Being on top of the speaker facing up, it's right where something can get pur or dropped on it, or a cat walking across it. The hard plastic seems much more resilient. It's also hard to tell on the sound, because the A5000 has two fewer speakers.

The top of this speaker is a textured plastic, like a car's dashboard. Not super fancy, but resilient. The A7000 has very shiny black plastic, which looks very nice and is easy to clean, but also lacks resilience and shows dust more readily.

The remote is infrared, so you need to have line of sight to the speaker for it to work, but it's full featured, even having buttons to control optional additional speakers. which I really appreciate.

The instruction book is pretty good. Setup is easy, especially if you connect it to a television. It'll put the menus right up on the screen. It's really built to be a television speaker with bluetooth and other inputs so it can be used for other things as a secondary purpose.

I'm still trying to figure out what I can do with the Chromecast feature that seems to be present in the speaker, but not in the television. So far I haven't had much luck connecting with Chromecast.

I definitely like the A7000 better, but there's a solid price difference. I love having a second HDMI input, since the way they've got these things set up, it outputs to my Sony television rather than the other way around, so I need to plug in extra devices to the soundbar, not the television, which makes it a weird decision to put so many more ports on the television than the speaker.

Great speaker, but still plenty of things that could be improved in a future version, like more satellite speaker compatibility, some kind of port passthrough from television, chromecast video, etc.
text_fidelity_b: Sony HT-A5000 5.1.2ch Dolby Atmos Sound Bar Surround Sound Home Theater with DTS:X and 360 Spatial Sound Mapping, works with Alexa and Google Assistant,Black

text_fidelity_a:
Logitech MX Vertical Wireless Mouse – Advanced Ergonomic Design Reduces Muscle Strain, Control and Move Content Between 3 Windows and Apple Computers (Bluetooth or USB), Rechargeable, Graphite I have a couple of vertical mice that I use with my various computer systems, and they really do help with wrist fatigue and pressure. I also have a very nice Logitech MX Ergo trackball which is my go-to device for all of my systems. With Logitech releasing this vertical mouse, I was very optimistic that I would have the perfect solution. I was sorely disappointed. This is the worst Logitech device I have used and I can’t recommend it.

I’ll start with the good aspects of it, and then I will get into what isn’t so good.

This device can be connected via wireless USB or by Bluetooth. This is handy for when you want to use multiple systems and want to connect to them, in different ways. If you already have another wireless Logitech device, it can connect to the receiver for that device, reducing the number of wireless ports required. It connects well through either method and I have been able to move it between systems just with the press of the connection button on top.

In operation, it seems to work well as a pointing device. I will say that if you are not used to working with a vertical mouse there is a learning curve that is involved and you will be very frustrated while you make the adjustment. The movement isn’t hard – it’s working with the buttons which even though are worked with the same fingers they feel unnatural at first. This is a problem with all vertical mice, not just this one.

It is rechargeable, meaning no more batteries, and it holds a charge for a good while. I like mice and keyboards that don’t need batteries as in the very long term it saves money. (Logitech has a solar keyboard that is phenomenal and never needs to be plugged in at all – great device.)

I have three main issues with this vertical mouse. The first is the build quality. It feels very lightweight and cheap, and I would call it fragile. It is supposed to be light and maneuverable so it’s easy to use, but it’s so much so that it has a very cheap feel to it that is unsettling. Second, this is a HUGE mouse which for me is great but for most people is unworkable. It fits my hand very well, but I have hands like a gorilla. My wife tried it and found it to be completely unusable because she couldn’t work the buttons well at all due to the size. Finally, this is a very expensive peripheral compared to other vertical mice I have used that I actually prefer. This vertical mouse presently sells here for about $100. I have one that cost around $25 at the time I bought it, feels more solid and is easier to use. My wife and I compared the Logitech vertical mouse with my cheaper one, and we both agreed that the less expensive one was easier to handle and worked just as well. The only thing I lose with the cheaper mouse is Bluetooth connectivity, which in my case is not a deal breaker.

I wish I could rate this mouse more highly but I just can’t. It’s expensive, feels cheap and just isn’t made to fit smaller hands (and usually, it’s a challenge finding mice for larger hands). It’s worth consideration if you need a mouse that can be easily transitioned between wireless and Bluetooth, but if you just need to use it with one system I’d recommend researching other options before making a purchase.
text_fidelity_b: Logitech MX Vertical Wireless Mouse – Advanced Ergonomic Design Reduces Muscle Strain, Control and Move Content Between 3 Windows and Apple Computers (Bluetooth or USB), Rechargeable, Graphite

Garmin nüvi 360 3.5-Inch Bluetooth Portable GPS Navigator with Text-To-Speech (Discontinued by Manufacturer) I've had this Nuvi 360 since Dec, 2006. It really works well. I carried it with me to DC. Even on foot it was terrific. It knew where all the restaurants and points of interest were and faithfully navigated us around the ancient horse paths of the Virginia/DC area. Believe me, when you pop out of an underground Metro station in the middle of the night and have no idea where you are or which direction to head off in, the ol' Garmin was there.

It's so small it easily fits in a pocket. The built-in battery lasts reasonably long. In the car, the 12-Volt adapter allows the unit to stay on indefinitely. You can select which accent and which gender you want the voice prompts to speak. Australian "Bruce," American "Jill" and a host of other combinations. All very fun. The voice prompts are the best. You really don't need to look at the thing while driving because it's uncanny in telling you what to do when you need to do it. It is amazingly accurate: something like 20 feet. It takes you right to the destination driveway.

It acquires the sats quickly and doesn't get flustered if you violate its recommendation and go in a different route. It just says, "recalculating" and finds another route for you. None of this "make a U-turn, bonehead!" It gives you enough time to make the turns, too. Also, it displays how far it is until the next turn. Very nice. No need to worry if you've missed it.

If you are planning on going to Europe, buy the unit that comes preloaded with both US and Europe maps as purchasing the Europe maps after the fact will really jump the cost unnecessarily.

I haven't used the Bluetooth capability yet but might later...after I get a Bluetooth phone.

The display is quite viewable in daylight and very bright at night, though it can be set to auto-dim at sundown so it's not too bright at night. You can touch the screen and scroll the map under your finger much like Google Maps can, to preview your route if desired. It shows coordinates and you can save them as destinations if desired, even if the location doesn't have an official street address. It is an MP3 player and can display photos and play Audible books on tape. When you are using the MP3 or Audible features, it pauses the file playing back to announce directions, then returns to the file without losing any of the MP3 file or book info. Very nice.

At extra cost, it has the ability to add foreign language dictionaries which can verbally speak phrases and words to you. You can also add Travel Guides and other software via the SD chip slot.

Overall, I'm very pleased with this device. It's accurate, fast, functional and small.

The one thing that doesn't work is the windshield suction mount. It broke before I even used it once. The plastic loops on the suction cup that receive the ball arm's hinge pin are too thin and fragile and broke with just a little normal hinge adjustment.

I recommend the model 010-10908-00 friction mount that looks like a bean bag with a ball arm sticking up. I made something similar by taking an unneeded 1/4" thick mousepad and epoxying a couple of small 1" x 1" angle brackets to the pad to hold the ball arm that I salvaged from the broken suction cup mount.

A friction mount is interchangeable with multiple vehicles, doesn't slide around on the dash and allows complete and rapid removal and/or hiding to avoid theft. Plus, you don't have to glue a disk to the dash for the suction cup to attach to.

UPDATE 10-22-07:
The 360 works well enough; better than most. It should: Five point three bills should deliver one heck of a map!

I've had it since Dec 2006...less than one year. Today I get an offer from Garmin to update my North American map software for a mere point seven bills. That's AFTER the five point three bills I already sunk into this little electronic gizmo.

I heard Garmin has a one year free map update policy, but their website won't let me do it. Not cool. The cost of the unit has already fallen significantly from what I originally paid and now they want more to get it current, within a year of purchase. Not cool at all. Also, impossible to contact by email. Garmin website is in a permanent loop back to itself when clicking on the "contact by email" option. Otherwise, it's call and wait on hold between certain times. Not cool again.

Then a friend says how well his Verizon GPS works on his wireless phone. I look into that. Verizon offers a full time GPS cost and a single use option for under three bucks per use.

For what I have wasted on this Garmin--over five bills and counting upward forever with their unfriendly updates--that's a whole heck of a lot of one-time Verizon uses with what will be the most updated, most accurate database. After all, no one's going to beat the phone company with accurate phone numbers and addresses.

If I hadn't already bought into the Garmin ripoff, I'd definitely go with Verizon's phone based GPS: the phone will always be with you when you need it instead of in the glove compartment in the other car.

And it most likely won't get stolen. It's a darned pain to have to put the Garmin away after each use so some cretin won't bash in a window to steal a very, very expensive toy that could just as easily fit inside a phone.

Go with the phone.
text_fidelity_b: Garmin nüvi 360 3.5-Inch Bluetooth Portable GPS Navigator with Text-To-Speech (Discontinued by Manufacturer)

Dell Inspiron Gaming PC Desktop AMD Ryzen 7 2700 Processor, 16GB DRAM, 1TB HDD, AMD Radeon RX 580 4GB GDDR5 Graphics Card, Windows 10 64-bit, Blue LED, Model Number: i5676-A696Blu I benchmarked using 3DMark, Time spy. From the results you can see it falls about where you would expect for its hardware and pricepoint. You are going to do better than an entry level gaming laptop, but you aren't going to be blowing anyone out of the water. But... this comp isn't really made for high performance.

It did handle both Minecraft and Ark. If you have kids you may have run into issues with Minecraft being RAM greedy, which is why you want at least 8GB and this has 16GB. So it will handle it with most mods pretty well.

Ark is terrible on computers. Even high end gaming rigs can struggle with it. It is one of the reasons I used it for testing. It is so poorly optimized that it will crash your PC and chuckle at your demise. This computer handled it well on medium settings, which isn't too bad. I wouldn't run epic settings on anything short of a NASA computer, and even still I'd be worried it would crash the space station or accidentally launch missiles.

Bottomline; this computer will make most games playable, they will not be "epic". It's a decent entry level gaming computer. I am not going to tell you to build your own if you want to save money and get a better set up for the same amount. Honestly, if you were of the mindset to do that you would not be considering $700 Dell computers. I have built my own computer, I have also wanted to throw it on the lawn and light it on fire, because when something goes wrong I have no one to blame but myself, and no one to fix it either. So... ignore the "build it yourself" shamers. You do you. If you want to buy an entry level gaming computer go for it. I would strongly recommend saving up the additional $250 to get the upgraded version of this computer though. For not much more, you get a whole heck of a lot more computer. Better processor, better graphic card, way better storage, and an SSD to run your operating system.

I knocked a star for the price and because the driver update software they have on there is a joke. I had to go manually update drivers myself. If that's not your deal I recommend adding a 3rd party driver updater, do not rely on Dells. If you are feeling brave you can buy a more powerful gaming computer for $700, you will just have to do a bit more research that they are a legitimate company.
text_fidelity_b: Dell Inspiron Gaming PC Desktop AMD Ryzen 7 2700 Processor, 16GB DRAM, 1TB HDD, AMD Radeon RX 580 4GB GDDR5 Graphics Card, Windows 10 64-bit, Blue LED, Model Number: i5676-A696Blu

GAOMON PD1560 15.6 Inches 8192 Levels Pen Display with Arm Stand 1920 x 1080 HD IPS Screen Drawing Tablet with 10 Shortcut Keys TL:DR - if you want a good tablet from a brand that cares about it's customers/users AND has good drivers/software in a 16" screen you can't go wrong with this device. Huion Kamvas Pros are good and all, but I've heard too many issues compared to this device with virtually none. Especially considering the total cost is around 350 - 375.

It's not perfect and pickier users like me may not like some of the workarounds, but for a first art tablet that is basically what I'd consider the best package and/or intro into digital art you can't go wrong.

The GAOMON PD1560 really surprised me with it's performance to price ratio. The device itself is light weight and comes with what I would dub as a starter bundle of accessories. Tablet, Stand, Glove, Nibs, Carrying case, etc. The line quality is also really amazing and when running my tests didn't notice any abnormal line wobble if any at all. Brad Coblow does a good review of it. Contratry to his review the quality isn't bad at all. If you've handled a computer monitor this tablet feels like it more or less. Drivers weren't an issue and the hot keys were fantastic.

The pen kept a great charge and felt nice to use along with the included artist glove (I got only a single two finger one). Drawing without the screen protector was a little squeaky at times, but had no issue in CS6 and CSP. The tablet stays nearly completely when you adjust the brightness/backlit to sub 65 degrees F. Luckily it doesn't change the looks all that much. There is a bit of parallax and calibration can take some time to get completely right but pen accuracy is top notch.

Screen quality is good and the cables are pretty rigid so no worries there. They actually connect by recessing into a slot rather than on the edge of the device.

Lastly is customer service. I really enjoyed GAOMON's customer service which I wish more companies would do.

There are a few caveats though. To get the pen the most accurate no matter where you point on the screen you need to understand where you touch the dot when calibrating. Next you need to hold the pen in the exact same orientation and way when you draw. That means holding the pen the exact same way with little deviation of that angle to get things to line up as well as say an iPad Pro. If you don't the distance when you calibrate really well is under say... 0.5mm or less. I am really stingy about this, but for someone who isn't this isn't a big thing to worry about.

Next are the hotkeys which act more like a macbook's butterfly keyboard in terms of presses. They press well and have very little travel almost like the old iphone home buttons. This may bother some, but didn't for me. I did need to place some tape with texture to understand where my buttons were without looking.

The screen protector I didn't install and I found it really annoying to even attempt to install. Then again I've written with fountain pens for 5 years now so am very used to buttery smooth pen work.
text_fidelity_b: GAOMON PD1560 15.6 Inches 8192 Levels Pen Display with Arm Stand 1920 x 1080 HD IPS Screen Drawing Tablet with 10 Shortcut Keys

text_fidelity_a:
Polk Audio PSW505 12" Powered Subwoofer, 460 Watts(300 Watts RMS) & Amazon Basics Subwoofer Cable, 25ft This is pretty heavy, but not so large that it's hard to position. I have it next to my computer that I use to listen to Amazon streaming MP3 music. My main speakers are NHT Model Twos, and this subwoofer supplies an excellent bottom end to the music. I haven't played it loud yet, but I'm looking forward to trying it out on a movie soundtrack.

The power switch has three positions -- Off, On, and Auto. In the Auto setting, it turns itself on if it senses an incoming signal. When I'm playing music softly, I'm finding that it takes a while to discover that it should turn on. In my case, the subwoofer is sitting next to my desk, and it's not hard to reach the power switch. But keep this in mind if you want to hide it somewhere that would make the power switch hard to reach. (It's near the top of the rear of the cabinet.) There's also a phase switch, with two positions. There's no magic to that; just set it to the position that sounds best. As with all subwoofers, the placement in your room isn't critical, although the subwoofer's sound can be somewhat amplified if you locate it in a corner.

Update: I've had time now to use this with lots of different types of music, as well as TV and movies. The bass is very solid and tight, with no boominess at all. It blends beautifully, with plenty of power for my medium-sized room. This is very musical, adding firm support that's more than just "punch". This is surely one of the best values in powered subwoofers, and I'd buy it again in a heartbeat.
text_fidelity_b: Polk Audio PSW505 12" Powered Subwoofer, 460 Watts(300 Watts RMS) & Amazon Basics Subwoofer Cable, 25ft

text_fidelity_a:
Soundcore Wakey Bluetooth Speaker Powered by Anker with Alarm Clock, Stereo Sound, FM Radio, White Noise, QI Wireless Charger with 7.5W Charging for iPhone and 10W for Samsung I ordered the 'Soundcore Wakey Bluetooth Speaker Powered by Anker with Alarm Clock, Stereo Sound, FM Radio, White Noise, QI Wireless Charger with 7.5W Charging for iPhone and 10W for Samsung' for review and would like to share some of my thoughts after a few weeks.

First off, this thing is actually pretty amazing. The build quality is nice and aesthetically it looks clean. The sound quality is nice but not phenomenal. However for how small it is, it does produce decent sound and for a bedside alarm clock it does quite well. The wireless charging works great for my Galaxy Note 8 (and does in fact Fast-Charge) however there have been a couple nights to where my phone was not charged the next morning. The fast charger also works with my wireless earbuds which I attached an image showing the charge light on the Wakey, and the wireless earbuds case indicating charging. However for the wireless earbud charging, it does take some precise positioning to get them to charge. I noticed in other review that others weren't happy with the bright display light with no way to adjust it any dimmer than the lowest setting, however they must have updated that with a firmware update (which was super easy to do) as I had no issues with the display being too bright at night. I use the auto adjust setting which seems to work quite well as far as I can tell. Also I love the sleep mode sounds that you can adjust several (or just one) sound volumes to create your own personalized preference. I do wish that there were more sound options but the ones they provide are acceptable. I also wish that you could download and install more alarm sounds. Bluetooth connectivity is super quick and have never once had an issue with pairing it up to my phone. Really the ONLY issue I have with the Wakey is that to get the sleep mode sounds going, you need to connect with the app, and via Bluetooth connect to the device. No big deal right? Well my concern is that you will need to keep it connected for this feature to work. This means you will be connected to the Wakey ALL night and this kind of bugs me. It's just kind of creepy that the Wakey is connected to your phone all night while you sleep. I wish there was a way to just play your favorite white noise sleep sound by pressing a button on the Wakey device without having to always connect and stay connected to the app and your phone. The other gripe is that the plug design is huge and makes it so that I have had to move my nightstand further way from the wall to use it. Other than those two gripes, and the only reason for docking one star, the Soundcore Wakey is a very good product and a really great value.
*On a side note - I just tested the Wakey while watching some Youtube videos and the latency is not so good. There is quite a bit of delay and the voices do not sync up at all so I wouldn't recommend using the Wakey for listening to videos.
text_fidelity_b: Soundcore Wakey Bluetooth Speaker Powered by Anker with Alarm Clock, Stereo Sound, FM Radio, White Noise, QI Wireless Charger with 7.5W Charging for iPhone and 10W for Samsung

So they must have made some useful advances in the relevant technology in the four years since I last purchased a transmitter from them.

I have tested this transmitter with multiple Bluetooth headphones that I own, and in each case, the Bluetooth connects seamlessly. I like the fact that the transmitter speaks and lets me know when the Bluetooth has connected. And a split second after that, the sound from my TV comes through my Bluetooth headphones. My old Avantree transmitter had neither of those abilities. It would take up to 2 minutes to get it connected to my Bluetooth headphones after multiple tries, and the sound's clarity and volume weren't nearly as good.

As was the case with my previous transmitter, this one can handle multiple Bluetooth headphones at the same time. So far I have only attempted transmission with two at a time.

Finally, the appearance of this transmitter is much fancier than the old one. I will admit that it is about three times larger than the old one, but that is not really a problem for me, because the old one was tiny and this one is still conveniently small. It has some cute, space-age looking little antennas on it that the other one didn't have, which may partially account for why it works so much better.

All in all, I am very pleased with this purchase.

text_fidelity_a:
UltraPro 8K HDMI 2.1 Cable, 6ft. High Speed 48Gbps, 8K @ 60Hz, 4K 1440p 1080p @ 120Hz, HDR VRR eARC QMS, Compatible with PS5 Xbox Series X Roku TV, Streaming, TV, Monitor, All HDMI Devices, 57347 Note: the 4K term is marketing, just about all consumer devices are UHD (2160p). So I'm going to use the UHD term, feel free to translate to "format commonly referred to as 4K" if you prefer.

I tested this cable on my newest UHD tv, with streaming UHD video from multiple sources, and then with a UHD nature documentary on a bluray player. I'd been using a very good 18Gb ("4K") cable before, so possibly a side-by-side test wouldn't show any difference. But I did immediately notice how sharp and bright the picture was in both cases, so I can at least say that this makes a very good video cable for UHD.

The cable is well made and feels sturdy, with a nice grab handle at each end, and inserts just the way it should into HDMI ports, with neither wiggle nor overmuch tightness. I didn't notice any minor flaws that might make me concerned about build quality, and I would expect it to last, at least until it becomes obsolete.

What should you buy if you don't have any so-called 8K media or devices, like most of us, and don't see them in your immediate future? In that case I'd just go with very good "4K" or "8K" cables, but without paying premium prices. The product description might say "Premium High Speed HDMI Cable" (18Gbps) or "Ultra High Speed HDMI Cable" (48Gbps). The first corresponds to the HDMI 2.0b standard, the second to HDMI 2.1.
text_fidelity_b: UltraPro 8K HDMI 2.1 Cable, 6ft. High Speed 48Gbps, 8K @ 60Hz, 4K 1440p 1080p @ 120Hz, HDR VRR eARC QMS, Compatible with PS5 Xbox Series X Roku TV, Streaming, TV, Monitor, All HDMI Devices, 57347

Osprey Apogee Men's Laptop Backpack , Kraken Blue This is a nice backpack. It’s lightweight and the color is very cool. It’s like a blue grey with dark teal straps. It’s not flashy but it’s not boring black either.
The 2 bottle holders on the side are very sleek and well done. It’s always annoying when bottles fall out is the side because they are too small - that won’t happen with these.
There are 3 pockets. The stash pocket is the only pocket that can be accessed if the compression hooks are used. The compression hooks can be tucked away when they aren’t needed which is nice - I don’t like having a bunch of hooks out catching on things.
The stash pocket isn’t huge but it’s a good size - can fit hand in easily and then it’s about 11” across.
The 2nd area is deep but isn’t wide. It will hold a jacket or sweater and then has 3 slotted pockets for a phone/ passport/ notebook. Outer 2 pockets are 3.5” and middle pocket is 4” wide. All pockets are about 5.5” deep.
The middle compartment also has a red clip. It’s easy to use and I like to use these to attach my keys so they don’t drop to the bottom of bags.
The main compartment is pretty big.
It has a double sided padded laptop area that measures 10.5” wide.
On top of the laptop is a tablet area that is single sided padded that measures 10” wide and up to 13” tall. The tablet area isn’t as deep as the laptop area. This area would also work for documents.
The top handle is well padded and sewn. Below that there is a two sided opening for headphone cords or even a plug to charge your laptop/tablet.
The main straps are well padded and adjustable. They have a top strap and a lower strap for comfort and security.
The zippers are all well quality and have a material flap over the top so it should keep anything inside pretty dry.
text_fidelity_b: Osprey Apogee Men's Laptop Backpack , Kraken Blue

Echo Show 8 (1st Gen, 2019 release) -- HD smart display with Alexa – stay connected with video calling - Sandstone I purchased this for two reasons: a convenient way to display recipes that didn't require my phone being out, and streaming movies for when I'm in the kitchen for hours at a time.

I rely heavily on streaming during the holiday seasons while I bake to fulfill orders, and while the video quality was good, and the sound was AMAZING, the rest of the device was too troublesome to be worth it.
Example: Open amazon video, and it gives you 4 categories to go through, or your library. I go to my library (severe lag every single time) and I find the movie I want. I hit play, severe lag again, and it plays. Quality is not bad at all, especially for the price, but heaven forbid you have to pause. Once you pause for ~2-3 minutes, it goes to a screen saver. And when you unlock it, you have to go through the process of finding the movie all over again. It's a pain in the butt. They could at least have a "continue watching..." at the beginning of the prime menu, but it doesn't.

Secondly, our household has 3 users on our hulu account--if there was a way to switch users through the Echo, I didn't see it. I googled it, thinking I was overlooking it, and nothing. We all have very different tastes for shows/movies, and never use each others accounts for this reason. To have not one, but two streaming services being out of the question/too inconvenient to use, I couldn't handle it.

The integration was wonky at best. I have an echo dot that resides on a window sill about 3 feet from where I had my echo. My echo was off for voice recognition, but when I'd talk to my dot, it would display on my echo. This was cool except for two things: 1. It did it intermittently. 1 out of 3 times it would mirror to the echo. 2. if you were streaming something when the echo mirrored what the dot was telling you, guess what, YOU HAVE TO FIND THE MOVIE AGAIN. It was a nightmare.

Maybe down the road they'll figure out a more user friendly programming for this, but until then I'm returning it. It was meant to be a gift for family, but if I, an electronic savvy 30-something, can't figure it out, I wouldn't be comfortable giving it to my grandparents, which was the end goal.
text_fidelity_b: Echo Show 8 (1st Gen, 2019 release) -- HD smart display with Alexa – stay connected with video calling - Sandstone

text_fidelity_a:
Fujifilm X-E2 16.3 MP Mirrorless Digital Camera with 3.0-Inch LCD - Body Only (Silver) I've only had the Fujifilm X-E2 camera and 18-55mm lens for a short while and I've barely scratched the surface of it's capabilities. This is a camera anyone can use right out of the box but also one that you can spend years learning to master.

The retro look and styling are very attractive but they made it, for me at least who was used to an extended grip on the camera body, a little hard to handle. I found myself hitting the AE-L and AF-L buttons often and frequently by accident spun the exposure compensation dial without even realizing I had. I resolved this with the LensMate Thumb Grip designed for the X-E1/E2. It made a good camera great. I also added LensMate's brass soft release button to the shutter release. It does aid in smoother pressing of the shutter button but it also looks great on the camera.

The 18-55mm lens that comes with the X-E2 is a real pleasure to use. The zoom is stiff enough to let you feel in control but easy enough that you don't need brute force to use it.

Image quality, even at 100%, is outstanding. I've been getting so many 'keepers' that I've had to reevaluate my shooting style. I feel like I'm overshooting. In the past I was shooting three or four hundred images in an outing and getting maybe four or six shots I really want to keep and share. Now, with the X-E2 I'm finding two, three even four times that many shots that are worth keeping. I'm going to need a bigger hard drive!

Battery life has been pretty good for me. Even shooting in temperatures down in the 30's and 40's I had no problem taking well over three hundred images and still having battery bars left. In the times I've gone out all day wandering around the county I've yet to have to swap out the battery though I did purchase an extra just to have around.

Functionality, configurability and controls are extensive and a bit quirky but easy enough to get used to. As an example the Q button gives you 'Q'uick access to many of the more necessary and often used controls. You navigate around the Q menu with the 5-way controller but you make setting changes with the command dial. One of the features I found most interesting was the ability to constrain the ISO in Auto mode and set a minimum shutter speed. I also liked the ability to configure the four letter prefix for file names. All the 'extra' settings like special effects, double exposure, movie mode and panorama are accessed through the Drive button.

I did find a couple small negatives. Nothing to cause me not to want to use it but made me wonder. The odd menu systems. The pop-up flash is a bit anemic and is somewhat blocked by the 18-55mm lens. It's even worse when the hood is attached. The shoulder strap that comes with the camera... I know they're usually bad but this is cheap camera bad not quality camera bad. I put it around my neck, gave a tug, and then threw it away without putting it on the camera. I expected a little more quality there. The tulip lens hood that comes with the 18-55mm feels hard and brittle. It too could have been a bit better quality. I already mentioned the LensMate thumb grip that I think is an absolute must add item (it's really worth the cost). My big clumsy hands desperately needed it to aid in stability and control.

Where to start with a conclusion? This is an interesting mix of old school retro styling and modern camera technology. I think Fuji have really blended them together well. I can see myself enjoying this camera for years to come. Very highly recommended.

{Update}
Not wanting to pile on the negatives but I had intended to and completely forgot to mention the battery door. It's really kind of flimsy and feels like it could easily break. Also, with the way it's hinged I find it rather hard to get the memory card out of the camera because it's so close and parallel to the battery door's hinge.
text_fidelity_b: Fujifilm X-E2 16.3 MP Mirrorless Digital Camera with 3.0-Inch LCD - Body Only (Silver)

Setup was as easy as with other Fire devices -- it walks you through the steps on screen. It also does a setup for having the remote control the TV and the receiver (my Fire Stick is plugged into my AV receiver). It works great -- I can power on/off both the TV (Samsung) and receiver (Onkyo) by just pressing the power button on the Fire remote. During power-up it also sets the receiver to the correct port for using the Fire stick. The volume on the remote controls the volume on the receiver. Very handy feature that works every time.

The overall speed and responsiveness is improved over earlier Fire sticks. Menus are more snappy and apps load faster. There are also a number of new settings to control audio and video aspects. I left most on their default, but it's nice to be able to get into the settings and tweak them.

A very nice upgrade to the Fire line. 100% satisfied with the purchase!

text_fidelity_a:
Samsung Electronics 840 EVO-Series 120GB 2.5-Inch SATA III Single Unit Version Internal Solid State Drive MZ-7TE120BW As of early 2014, this is the price/value drive to get, for a home system.

Yeah there is another drive that is as good for the same money, just sort on #of reviews or rating to have it come up. But this and that one are can't miss price/speed/value drives

I have this one in a Windows 7 machine, and it's use is transparent and I don't do all those tweaks you read about and I read all about them.

If you want to keep it simple unplug all drives but the DVD, if installing that way, and the SSD drive. Install windows 7. Profit. Than do two things. Make sure disk level indexing is off (which you should be doing anyway) this is under your C: drive properties right under where it says Compress this drive to save space. The indexing shouldn't be set if you installed the way I said, but check anyway. This will not effect windows indexing (which I vote for leaving on even on a SSD drive)

Then update your drives firmware.

Don't worry about cache and indexing, super fetch and all that. Just let Win 7 set all that all up. and all that.

Don't worry about hibernate. Use hibernate if you want, or don't, but you don't need to change it since you are running on a SSD. Same with system restore if you have the room, and you like having it on, leave it on. This drive will automatically over-provision 7% of the drive so you don't need to set that.

Windows will set up your drive just fine. If you want to go research it all and make your own decisions, that's fine I did the same thing. And the above 'simple' installation was what I decided on. (I did 3 separate installations working through various options).. I have tweaks I do, but they are tweaks I do SSD or no SSD.

A lot of information about SSD drives is based on small drives and older controllers. You don't need to worry about how long your drive will last. It will last longer than you will have your computer. Look up the tests on this on the internet to understand how little of an issue this really is. A lot of what is written about SSD's is written by enthusiasts/gamers who are into tweaking systems. If, like me, you like doing this kind of research, great. Otherwise just install windows and use your drive SDD drive like any other drive.
text_fidelity_b: Samsung Electronics 840 EVO-Series 120GB 2.5-Inch SATA III Single Unit Version Internal Solid State Drive MZ-7TE120BW

text_fidelity_a:
SanDisk 32GB Class 4 SDHC Memory Card, Frustration-Free Packaging- SDSDB-032G-AFFP (Label May Change) This review is of the 64GB SDHX card. I use it for a specific purpose: backing up my document folders on my two laptops. It works perfectly with my Windows XP systems over ancient USB 2.0 ports. I can still back up a full card in less than an hour, and if I were on a more modern system with USB 3.0 it would take only a fraction of that time.

This particular card will NOT work in my Samsung Galaxy Note II (I had to try anyway). In fact, make sure your device will actually accept SDHX cards before purchaing this 64GB model or you may be disappointed. Most Microsoft Windows systems running XP service pack 2 or later, Windows CE and Server 2003 will recognize this card, as will Mac OS X Snow Leopard 10.6.5 or later. Phones, tablets and devices running Microsoft Windows RT will also recognize this card. Beyond that check first.

Back to how I use this card: the price for this card is around forty bucks at the time of this review. I could have gotten an exernal hard drive in the terabyte range for twice that, but this has no moving parts, fits in my wallet and with a [[ASIN:B00FSDKBYY Sabrent SuperSpeed USB 3.0 Flash Memory Card Reader]] plugs into any computer (with an operating system that supports the format) via USB ports. For me it's convenient, especially since I am only backing up working documents and never come close to the 64GB capacity (which is closer to 56GB formatted.) In fact I use two of these in rotation for safety, overwriting the older one completely since it takes less than an hour. I always keep the other one on my person.

As the SDHX standard becomes more established and ubiquitous this type of card may work with more devices. At 64GB this is probably the smallest size since the SDHX format was designed to accomodate up to two terabytes. So unless you have a device that is compatible with this format, or you are using it for a single purpose on a supported operating system, you may want to get an SDHC card instead.
text_fidelity_b: SanDisk 32GB Class 4 SDHC Memory Card, Frustration-Free Packaging- SDSDB-032G-AFFP (Label May Change)

Samsung Galaxy Tab S 10.5-Inch Tablet (16 GB, Titanium Bronze) I love this tablet and, if it weren't for the battery life and how long it takes to recharge, I would give it 5 stars. The tablet itself is beautiful, thin, lightweight and works beautifully. I have had mine since the beginning of September 2014, and I have only had to reboot it twice since then (due to errors, I mean). The display is beautiful. The sound is quite good, for a tablet. And now that Samsung has allowed it to upgrade to Lollipop, I can run most of my new apps from my 32 gb SD Card and this leaves me a lot less nervous about running out of memory. Though, I still find the 16 GB HD a bit on the tight side overall.

My previous tablet was a Toshiba Excite AT305T16. It was my first tablet, but I still could tell how slow it was. And it constantly needed to be rebooted. Everything kept getting bound up on it. Not so with this Samsung. It is quick, it stays fresh, and it just plain performs. Which is all we ask for, right? I will be buying more Samsung products in the future, I think. Those guys really know and deliver quality. Now, if they could just improve the battery and be a bit more generous with the on-board memory.

UPDATE: I have downgraded my review by one star. I have owned this tablet since August of 2014. And, although I still enjoy it, I am now running out of memory and, even though I have a 64gb sd card attached, I am finding it increasingly challenging and frustrating to manage the remaining space. While many of the apps can be moved to the SD card, most of them can't. And the apps themselves are becoming larger and larger overall. And, to make matters worse, suddenly, I can no longer update many of my apps residing on the SD card, unless I move them back to the internal storage first. This is too laborious and time consuming and I haven't found a fix for it yet. Also, suddenly I can no longer move PDF files onto the SD card either. Other types of files can be moved as before, but not the PDF files. Wondering if the tablet performed some sort of automatic system upgrade that may have triggered these issues. When I "upgraded" (and I use that term lightly, with tongue in cheek) from Kitkat to Lollipop, the tablet lost some very useful functions. So now I have to wonder why these problems are suddenly cropping up?
text_fidelity_b: Samsung Galaxy Tab S 10.5-Inch Tablet (16 GB, Titanium Bronze)

Incipio Highland Folio Case for Fire Phone, Black I had noticed that a huge percentage of people in the Middle East have folio cases for their phones, but I've seen so few here in the States that this was a big surprise to me. I like the idea a lot if you're keeping this in a purse or a pocket with a bunch of other stuff, but I've long ago reserved an entire pocket for my phone. In the case of a pocket, all this added texture actually makes it harder to get the phone out. And I can see the drawback others' mention about it not keeping itself shut; this could be a problem in the case of a purse with keys and all kinds of junk rolling around in there.

I really like the materials, however, to include the thin metal backing and the faux leather front. It stands up fine for a phone, but when you're already adding this amount of thickness, it seems like you could build some stopping points into the inside front cover. Of course that would mess up the credit card pocket. And speaking of that pocket, it seems like a good idea, if you can refrain from cramming so much into it that your phone becomes your wallet. I have another pocket on most pants, which I reserve for my wallet and keys; makes me wonder how other people live in such disorganization.

It's a pretty good quality product, and I suspect if you're looking for a folio case, you won't find one better. However, the point of the cover not staying shut is valid and maybe a reason to continue your research.
text_fidelity_b: Incipio Highland Folio Case for Fire Phone, Black

text_fidelity_a:
4K HDR HDMI Switch, Koopman 5 Ports 4K 60Hz HDMI 2.0 Switcher Selector with IR Remote, Supports Ultra HD Dolby Vision, High Speed (Max to 18.5Gbps), HDR10, HDCP 2.2 & 3D (I have received this product mostly free in exchange for an honest review)
I have been using a 3-in to 1-out HDMI switch for a couple years and recently the media box for one of my TVs died, so put on connected to the single HDMI input. It works just fine, but I have more than 3 devices I'd like to connect and reaching to change the input is annoying.
This has solved multiple problems. having 5 HDMI inputs is a pretty sweet deal. I've only tested 3 of them so far and they work just fine. One nice feature that I didn't expect is that it doesn't appear to let you switch to an input that doesn't have a device even powered on, at least using the remote.
The picture quality is just fine. I have nothing to compare it to, but it looks no worse than it ever did.
The nice feature of my previous switch was that it did not need to be powered. The Koopman one DOES need power. It comes with the micro USB cable and power adapter, but if your TV has an open 5v usb output, that might be more convenient. I had to plug it in. It's a minor annoyance, but if you're low on outlet space, keep it in mind.
It's small and light, so I'll need to anchor it in place so it's not flying off the stand. HDMI cables like to pull things awry. It's almost inconspicuous.
Speaking of HDMI cables, it doesn't come with one. I had expected (and didn't pay attention to the product description - so MY bad) at least a short one.
The remote is tiny. This is great because it doesn't take up much space, but I KNOW I'm going to spend a bunch of events looking for it in the couch or under the footrest or because a spider dragged it into their web in the corner. The remote worked from at least 15-20 feet away (as far as I could comfortably go), BUT, the angle of reception is not very wide. It might be about 60 degrees (I did not pull out the protractor). The box itself had a button on it, so if the remote goes temporarily missing, you can still tap your way between inputs.
I'll give it some time to see how it lasts. If it does well over time, I'll possibly buy another for another TV with only one HDMI input.
One cool improvement would be if it had an audio output, even in only a 1/8" port.
text_fidelity_b: 4K HDR HDMI Switch, Koopman 5 Ports 4K 60Hz HDMI 2.0 Switcher Selector with IR Remote, Supports Ultra HD Dolby Vision, High Speed (Max to 18.5Gbps), HDR10, HDCP 2.2 & 3D

Nikon AF-S DX NIKKOR 55-300mm f/4.5-5.6G ED Vibration Reduction Zoom Lens with Auto Focus for Nikon DSLR Cameras This is my current go-to lens. I wish I could afford one of the more fancy-schmancy professional telephotos, but until then, this one is the one parked on my Nikon D7000.

Uses:

1. Birds, bugs and other critters from a safe distance or on the fly/run
2. Portraits of one or two people (gives excellent bokeh)
3. Landscapes and seascapes, especially in vertical/portrait mode.

Limitations:

1. Buildings from across-the-street distance
2. Large groups of people
3. Macro shots from thisclose

Depending on the type of photography you enjoy, this may or may not be the lens for you. It works fine for me for the uses above, especially when the subjects are a respectable distance away, but it doesn't have a wide enough angle for limitations 1 and 2, and if you're closer than a couple of feet it won't focus properly.

It's also pretty heavy, but makes up for this by making you look like a pro who knows what they're about, especially when you use the lens hood (included and highly recommended for use)

The auto-focus is not as smooth as it should be, and you can sometimes hear the mechanism moving around trying to do its job, but image stabilization and the tripod detection mode are huge pluses. (It also attaches/detaches from the camera in the opposite direction to my other (Sigma) lens)

For the type of photography I'm doing at the moment. even if it's not on the camera, this lens goes with me wherever I roam.

Amanda Richards, March 30, 2012
text_fidelity_b: Nikon AF-S DX NIKKOR 55-300mm f/4.5-5.6G ED Vibration Reduction Zoom Lens with Auto Focus for Nikon DSLR Cameras

Neewer TT560 Flash Speedlite for Canon Nikon Panasonic Olympus Pentax and Other DSLR Cameras，Digital Cameras with Standard Hot Shoe Failed to flash about every 25th go. When it did flash, output was inconsistent - often a half a stop darker.

I purchased this just to use as a slave to be triggered by another flash - a Yongnuo 560-II. I figured this one looked pretty similar and cost a lot less (though it's less powerful and doesn't have zooming or an LCD screen, doesn't go into sleep mode. I didn't need those things). The Yongnuo was about $60 and this one was $37 at the time.

I would should 100 shots of the same setup with the same 2 flashes -- everything the same (this was for macro - close up work). Over and over again I'd find dark frames on the Neewer TT560 side and the Yongnuo was dead on every time.

If you're shooting your nephew's 5th Birthday Party and don't care if the shots come out (why aren't you using a phone cam?), then this is OK. If you care at all, pay the $25 extra and get the Yongnuo. (Actually, Yongnuo has a 460-ii model for about $40. I haven't tried that, but I'd give it a shot before this one).

text_fidelity_a:
Fujifilm Instax Mini 26 + Rainbow Film Bundle - Black A long time ago I had access to a Polaroid Instamatic camera. It was great - snap a picture, it spits out a sheet. Wait about 2 minutes and what you have is a printed photograph. Polaroid is gone now (though the name gets licensed over and over again), and with it went all of the film for the camera that made it so useful. This new camera by Fuji brings back some of the fun of instant photos, though it is by no means perfect and it suffers from some of the same issues the older Polaroid camera had.

The idea is very straightforward - point-and-shoot, and the camera ejects an exposure that will develop over a few moments and will be fully developed in approximately 2 minutes. This is great for social events and is a fun way to share candid shots. The camera is very lightweight and it is small too so it is easy to pack and carry with you.

There are a few issues with the camera, though, some of which are very much like the old Polaroids of days gone by. The images do come out a bit grainy and are definitely not high resolution. If you are looking for images with nice, clean edge detail and bright, vibrant colors, this is going to disappoint you. Also, the images are really small, a little bigger than a passport picture but not by very much. And finally, the film is relatively expensive, a pack of exposures coming with only 10 slides and costing about $0.60 per exposure.

On the plus side, the camera is very easy to use and the camera body itself is not very expensive at all.

There are trade-offs with this camera. On one hand, it is super convenient, it’s fun and it’s relatively inexpensive. However, exposure quality is mediocre, pictures are small and on a per-picture basis the exposures are somewhat expensive. To me, the fun factor weighs heavily in favor of this camera and offsets some of the negatives. For social gatherings and recreational events, this is a fun camera and will serve well. Do not expect to have high-end results, though.
text_fidelity_b: Fujifilm Instax Mini 26 + Rainbow Film Bundle - Black
